claim: An estimated 15% of cancers worldwide are caused by infectious agents like viruses.
source: An estimated 15% of cancers worldwide are caused by infectious agents like viruses.
evidence: This is a general statement about cancer etiology that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was the first human tumor virus discovered.
source: Of these, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was the first human tumor virus discovered and is associated with malignancies of both B lymphocyte and epithelial cell origin.
evidence: This is a well-established historical fact in virology.

claim: EBV is associated with malignancies of both B lymphocyte and epithelial cell origin.
source: Of these, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was the first human tumor virus discovered and is associated with malignancies of both B lymphocyte and epithelial cell origin.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about EBV-associated cancers.

claim: T cells prevent the development of EBV-associated malignancies.
source: Normally, T cells prevent the development of EBV-associated malignancies and the virus persists quiescently in latently-infected memory B cells.
evidence: This is supported by established immunological knowledge about EBV control.

claim: EBV persists quiescently in latently-infected memory B cells.
source: Normally, T cells prevent the development of EBV-associated malignancies and the virus persists quiescently in latently-infected memory B cells.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about EBV latency.

claim: Nearly all adults in the world are latently infected with EBV.
source: As a result, nearly all adults in the world are latently infected (Longnecker et al., 2013), making EBV a particularly widespread and successful pathogen.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Longnecker et al., 2013.

claim: In the absence of a healthy immune system, EBV can transform B cells leading to markedly increased rates of lymphoma.
source: However, in the absence of a healthy immune system, such as following organ transplant or HIV infection, EBV can transform B cells leading to markedly increased rates of lymphoma in these populations.
evidence: This is supported by established clinical knowledge about EBV-associated lymphomas in immunocompromised patients.

claim: Primary human B cell infection in vitro by EBV leads to their growth transformation.
source: Primary human B cell infection in vitro by EBV leads to their growth transformation and serves as a model for oncogenesis in EBV-associated lymphomas.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about EBV transformation of B cells in culture.

claim: EBV-mediated B cell transformation requires the expression of six viral latent genes: EBNA1, EBNA2, EBNA-LP, EBNA3A, EBNA3C and LMP1.
source: This process requires the expression of six viral latent genes: Epstein-Barr Nuclear Antigen 1 (EBNA1), EBNA2, EBNA-LP, EBNA3A, EBNA3C and Latent Membrane Protein 1 (LMP1) (Longnecker et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Longnecker et al., 2013.

claim: EBNA2 is the major viral transcriptional activator and the first to be expressed upon infection.
source: EBNA2, the major viral transcriptional activator and the first to be expressed upon infection, upregulates expression of the other viral EBNA genes as well as host genes (Wang et al., 2000; Zimber-Strobl and Strobl, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2000 and Zimber-Strobl and Strobl, 2001.

claim: EBNA2 upregulates expression of the other viral EBNA genes as well as host genes.
source: EBNA2, the major viral transcriptional activator and the first to be expressed upon infection, upregulates expression of the other viral EBNA genes as well as host genes (Wang et al., 2000; Zimber-Strobl and Strobl, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2000 and Zimber-Strobl and Strobl, 2001.

claim: EBNA2 activates the expression of the viral oncoprotein LMP1.
source: EBNA2 also activates the expression of the viral oncoprotein LMP1, which drives the immortalization of the infected B cell into a lymphoblastoid cell line, or LCL, that proliferates indefinitely in culture.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about EBNA2 function.

claim: LMP1 drives the immortalization of the infected B cell into a lymphoblastoid cell line (LCL) that proliferates indefinitely in culture.
source: EBNA2 also activates the expression of the viral oncoprotein LMP1, which drives the immortalization of the infected B cell into a lymphoblastoid cell line, or LCL, that proliferates indefinitely in culture.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about LMP1 function in B cell transformation.

claim: The EBV latent oncoproteins mimic key aspects of normal B cell biology, promote proliferation, and inhibit the host innate tumor suppressor response to uncontrolled proliferation.
source: Together, the EBV latent oncoproteins mimic key aspects of normal B cell biology, promote proliferation, and inhibit the host innate tumor suppressor response to uncontrolled proliferation (Allday, 2013; Price and Luftig, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Allday, 2013 and Price and Luftig, 2014.

claim: The LMP1 oncoprotein is necessary for continued LCL growth and survival.
source: It is well-established that the LMP1 oncoprotein is necessary for continued LCL growth and survival (Kaye et al., 1993; Zimber-Strobl et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kaye et al., 1993 and Zimber-Strobl et al., 1996.

claim: LMP1 mimics a pro-survival TNF receptor that signals constitutively through the NFκB pathway to promote proliferation and suppress apoptosis in transformed cells.
source: LMP1 mimics a pro-survival TNF receptor that signals constitutively through the NFκB pathway to promote proliferation and suppress apoptosis in transformed cells (Cahir-McFarland et al., 2000; Okan et al., 1995; Pratt et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cahir-McFarland et al., 2000, Okan et al., 1995, and Pratt et al., 2012.

claim: Inhibition of the NFκB pathway activated downstream of LMP1 leads to apoptosis in LCLs.
source: In fact, inhibition of the NFκB pathway activated downstream of LMP1 leads to apoptosis in LCLs.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about NFκB signaling in LCLs.

claim: Early after infection, B cells rapidly proliferate despite low levels of LMP1 expression and NFκB activation.
source: However, recent work from our laboratory has demonstrated that, early after infection, B cells rapidly proliferate despite low levels of LMP1 expression and NFκB activation (Nikitin et al., 2010; Price et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nikitin et al., 2010 and Price et al., 2012.

claim: Early-infected cells show no overt signs of apoptosis despite strong activation of the cellular DNA damage response.
source: Surprisingly, these early-infected cells also show no overt signs of apoptosis despite strong activation of the cellular DNA damage response (Nikitin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nikitin et al., 2014.

claim: In early-infected cells, there is a viral-mediated mechanism independent of LMP1 signaling that promotes survival.
source: This suggests that in early-infected cells, there is a viral-mediated mechanism independent of LMP1 signaling that promotes survival.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that early-infected cells survive despite low LMP1 levels.

claim: The viral BCL-2 homologue BHRF1 confers chemoresistance in a mouse model of Burkitt lymphoma.
source: For example, the viral BCL-2 homologue BHRF1 confers chemoresistance in a mouse model of Burkitt lymphoma (BL) (Kvansakul et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kvansakul et al., 2010.

claim: The viral BHRF1 and BALF1 proteins exert non-redundant roles in protecting initially infected cells from apoptosis.
source: Similarly, the viral BHRF1 and BALF1 proteins exert non-redundant roles in protecting initially infected cells from apoptosis (Altmann and Hammerschmidt, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Altmann and Hammerschmidt, 2005.

claim: Expression of the EBNA3 proteins induces resistance to apoptosis in BL cells and primary B cells by downregulating Bim expression.
source: In addition, expression of the EBNA3 proteins induces resistance to apoptosis in BL cells and primary B cells by downregulating Bim expression (Paschos et al., 2009; Skalska et al., 2013), thereby making infected cells less 'primed' for apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Paschos et al., 2009 and Skalska et al., 2013.

claim: The EBNA3 family epigenetically downregulates human genes involved in cell cycle regulation and apoptosis.
source: The EBNA3 family is also known to epigenetically downregulate additional human genes involved in cell cycle regulation and apoptosis (Allday, 2013; Harth-Hertle et al., 2013; Hertle et al., 2009; Paschos et al., 2012; Skalska et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Allday, 2013; Harth-Hertle et al., 2013; Hertle et al., 2009; Paschos et al., 2012; Skalska et al., 2013.

claim: The EBNA3 proteins mediate epigenetic effects via interacting with additional proteins in such a way that chromatin architecture can be dramatically altered.
source: It has been shown that the EBNA3 proteins mediate these epigenetic effects, in part, via interacting with additional proteins in such a way that chromatin architecture can be dramatically altered (Bazot et al., 2015; McClellan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bazot et al., 2015 and McClellan et al., 2013.

claim: EBNA3 proteins can activate gene transcription in some instances.
source: While thought to be generally repressive in nature, recent work has shown that in some instances EBNA3 proteins can activate gene transcription (Bazot et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bazot et al., 2015.

claim: EBV-positive lymphomas are more difficult to treat than their EBV-negative counterparts.
source: In sum, viral proteins confer several survival advantages to infected cells, which often results in EBV-positive lymphomas that are more difficult to treat than their EBV-negative counterparts (Kelly et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kelly et al., 2006.

claim: The intrinsic apoptosis pathway is controlled by complex protein-protein interactions at the surface of mitochondria that regulate the release of cytochrome c.
source: The intrinsic apoptosis pathway is controlled by complex protein—protein interactions at the surface of mitochondria that regulate the release of cytochrome c (Youle and Strasser, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Youle and Strasser, 2008.

claim: BH3 profiling uses peptides derived from BH3-only pro-apoptotic proteins to identify the anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family members important for preventing apoptosis in a particular cell.
source: These functional interactions can be interrogated with an established approach called 'BH3 profiling', which uses peptides derived from BH3-only pro-apoptotic proteins to identify the anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family members important for preventing apoptosis in a particular cell (Del Gaizo Moore and Letai, 2013; Deng et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Del Gaizo Moore and Letai, 2013 and Deng et al., 2007.

claim: BH3 mimetics are highly specific small molecule inhibitors that promote apoptosis directly in sensitive cell types.
source: Furthermore, molecular characterization of the interface between BH3 domains of these proteins has allowed for the creation of a new class of small molecule inhibitors that promote apoptosis directly in sensitive cell types (Billard, 2013; Oltersdorf et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Billard, 2013 and Oltersdorf et al., 2005.

claim: BH3 mimetics show great promise in clinical trials.
source: These so-called 'BH3 mimetics' are highly specific and show great promise in clinical trials (Letai, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Letai, 2008.

claim: EBV infection of primary human B cells results in robust virus-mediated proliferation and activation of the pro-apoptotic DNA damage response with little expression of LMP1 during an early period after infection.
source: Previously, our laboratory has identified an early period after EBV infection of primary human B cells where, despite robust virus-mediated proliferation and activation of the pro-apoptotic DNA damage response, there is little expression of the key viral survival factor LMP1 (Price et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Price et al., 2012.

claim: Both latently infected cell populations (Prolif and LCL) are 100% EBV-positive.
source: Both latently infected cell populations are 100% EBV-positive as shown previously by immuno-fluorescence and fluorescent in situ hybridization (Nikitin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nikitin et al., 2010.

claim: EBV infection of primary B cells only modestly reduces overall mitochondrial priming.
source: BH3 profiling revealed that EBV infection of primary B cells only modestly reduces overall mitochondrial priming (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1 compare 10 µM Puma from B to Prolif and 1 µM Bim from B/Prolif to LCL).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Uninfected B cells depolarized their mitochondria upon treatment with Bad, Puma, or Bmf peptides, but not Noxa or Hrk peptides, indicating reliance on BCL-2 or BCL-w as a pro-survival BCL2 family member.
source: Uninfected B cells depolarized their mitochondria upon treatment with Bad, Puma, or Bmf peptides, but not Noxa or Hrk peptides, indicating reliance on BCL-2 or BCL-w as a pro-survival BCL2 family member (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and represents an inference from the BH3 profiling results.

claim: EBV-infected proliferating B cells (Prolif) lost sensitivity to the Bad peptide but remained sensitive to Puma and Bmf, supporting a survival mechanism reliant on both MCL-1 and BCL-2/BCL-w.
source: EBV-infected proliferating B cells (Prolif) lost sensitivity to the Bad peptide but remained sensitive to Puma and Bmf, supporting a survival mechanism reliant on both MCL-1, to block Bad-induced depolarization, and BCL-2/BCL-w, to block Noxa-induced depolarization (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and represents an inference from the BH3 profiling results.

claim: LCLs lost sensitivity to Bmf, but sensitivity to Puma did not change between Prolif and LCLs, suggesting additional BFL-1 mediated pro-survival effects in LCLs.
source: Finally, LCLs lost sensitivity to Bmf, but sensitivity to Puma did not change between Prolif and LCLs, suggesting additional BFL-1 mediated pro-survival effects in LCLs (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and represents an inference from the BH3 profiling results.

claim: EBV infection reduces the dependence of B cells on BCL-2, BCL-xL, or BCL-w for survival.
source: We hypothesized that EBV infection reduces the dependence of B cells on BCL-2, BCL-xL, or BCL-w for survival given the loss of Bad sensitivity between uninfected and early-infected B cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the BH3 profiling data.

claim: Treatment with ABT-737 concurrent with EBV infection resulted in an IC50 in proliferating B cells of ~10 nM.
source: Consistent with dependence of uninfected B cells on these BCL-2 family members predicted by BH3 profiling, treatment with ABT-737 concurrent with EBV infection resulted in an IC50 in proliferating B cells of ~10 nM (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: When ABT-737 was added to EBV-infected cells after the onset of virus-induced proliferation or to immortalized LCLs, an IC50 of ~2–4 µM was observed.
source: However, when ABT-737 was added to EBV-infected cells after the onset of virus-induced proliferation or to immortalized LCLs we observed high-level ABT-737 resistance with an IC50of ~2–4 µM (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: ABT-737 promoted apoptosis in uninfected B cells, while proliferating cells at 7 dpi and EBV transformed LCLs were resistant to apoptosis induction.
source: ABT-737 promoted apoptosis as measured by caspase 3/7 activity and Annexin V positivity in uninfected B cells, while proliferating cells at 7 dpi and EBV transformed LCLs were resistant to apoptosis induction (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: EBV induced potent resistance to ABT-199.
source: Similar to ABT-737, EBV induced potent resistance to ABT-199 (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: Uninfected human peripheral blood CD19+ B cells depend on BCL-2 for survival.
source: Therefore, uninfected human peripheral blood CD19+ B cells depend on BCL-2 for survival and EBV upregulates additional survival proteins to potently suppress apoptosis induced by BCL-2 antagonism.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ABT-199 sensitivity data.

claim: EBV upregulates additional survival proteins to potently suppress apoptosis induced by BCL-2 antagonism.
source: Therefore, uninfected human peripheral blood CD19+ B cells depend on BCL-2 for survival and EBV upregulates additional survival proteins to potently suppress apoptosis induced by BCL-2 antagonism.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the drug resistance data.

claim: MCL-1 mRNA increased from uninfected B to EBV-infected and proliferating B cells and was further increased in LCLs.
source: We observed that MCL-1 mRNA increased from uninfected B to EBV-infected and proliferating B cells and was further increased in LCLs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Both BCL-2 and BFL-1 were initially downregulated in early proliferating B cells relative to uninfected B cells, then upregulated during LCL outgrowth.
source: Over the same infection time course, both BCL-2 and BFL-1 were initially downregulated in early proliferating B cells relative to uninfected B cells, then upregulated during LCL outgrowth.
evidence: This is supported by data from the manuscript and prior transcriptomic analyses.

claim: BCL-2 and BFL-1 are both ultimately upregulated by EBV.
source: These data are consistent with prior transcriptomic analyses from our group (Price et al., 2012) and others indicating that BCL-2 and BFL-1 are both ultimately upregulated by EBV (D'Souza et al., 2004; Henderson et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Price et al., 2012, D'Souza et al., 2004, and Henderson et al., 1991.

claim: BCL-2 and MCL-1 protein levels mirror their respective mRNA expression levels during B cell outgrowth.
source: BCL-2 and MCL-1 protein levels mirror their respective mRNA expression levels during B cell outgrowth (Figure 3B, quantified in Figure 3C; note there is no viable BFL-1 antibody).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B and quantified in Figure 3C.

claim: ABT-737 resistance coincides with MCL-1 induction.
source: The aforementioned data indicate that ABT-737 resistance coincides with MCL-1 induction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between MCL-1 expression and ABT-737 resistance.

claim: When cells were treated with both A-1210 and either ABT-737 or ABT-199, early proliferating cells, but not LCLs, displayed elevated markers of apoptosis.
source: However, when cells were treated with both A-1210 and either ABT-737 or ABT-199, early proliferating cells, but not LCLs, displayed elevated markers of apoptosis (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: The combined action of ABT-199 and A-1210 supports the hypothesis that early-infected cells are more dependent upon MCL-1 and BCL-2 for survival than are LCLs.
source: The combined action of ABT-199 and A-1210 supports the hypothesis generated by BH3 profiling that early-infected cells are more dependent upon MCL-1 and BCL-2 for survival than are LCLs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the drug combination data.

claim: MCL-1 is a highly labile transcript and protein, and its expression is sensitive to RNA polymerase II stalling induced by CDK9 inhibition.
source: MCL-1 is a highly labile transcript and protein, and its expression is known to be sensitive to RNA polymerase II stalling induced by CDK9 inhibition (Gojo et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gojo et al., 2002.

claim: The CDK9 inhibitor, flavopiridol, induced rapid decreases in MCL-1 mRNA and protein, while leaving BCL-2 and BFL-1 levels largely unaffected.
source: Indeed, the CDK9 inhibitor, flavopiridol, induced rapid decreases in MCL-1 mRNA and protein, while leaving BCL-2 and BFL-1 levels largely unaffected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Early proliferating cells were more sensitive to apoptosis induced by a combination of flavopiridol and ABT-737 than LCLs.
source: Supporting our A-1210 data, we found that early proliferating cells were more sensitive to apoptosis induced by a combination of flavopirodol and ABT-737 than LCLs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) (Leverson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and a citation to Leverson et al., 2015.

claim: A clonal LCL with deletions in both BFL1 alleles was successfully generated using the CRISPR/Cas9 system.
source: We successfully generated a clonal LCL with deletions in both BFL1 alleles as assessed by Sanger sequencing (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The mutant ΔBFL-1 LCL expressed significantly reduced levels of BFL-1 mRNA as compared to WT LCL, LCL expressing Cas9 alone or Cas9-expressing LCLs targeting AAVS1 as a negative control.
source: These deletions were clearly evident by RT-PCR (Figure 3F), and, consequently, the mutant ΔBFL-1 LCL expressed significantly reduced levels of BFL-1 mRNA as compared to WT LCL, LCL expressing Cas9 alone or Cas9-expressing LCLs targeting AAVS1 as a negative control (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: ΔBFL-1 LCLs were significantly more sensitive to treatment with a combination of ABT-737 and A-1210 relative to WT, Cas9, or AAVS1 sgRNA control LCLs.
source: ΔBFL-1 LCLs were significantly more sensitive to treatment with a combination of ABT-737 and A-1210 relative to WT, Cas9, or AAVS1 sgRNA control LCLs (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: LCLs depend on BFL-1, MCL-1, and BCL-2 to protect from apoptosis induced by viral oncoprotein-driven proliferation.
source: These data support the hypothesis defined by our BH3 profiling data that LCLs depend on BFL-1, MCL-1, and BCL-2 to protect from apoptosis induced by viral oncoprotein-driven proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ΔBFL-1 LCL data combined with the BH3 profiling results.

claim: Mitogens such as the TLR9 ligand CpG DNA as well as CD40L/IL-4 promote B cell proliferation similar to EBV infection.
source: In cell culture, mitogens such as the TLR9 ligand CpG DNA as well as T cell derived CD40 ligand and IL-4 (CD40L/IL-4) promote B cell proliferation similar to EBV infection (Elgueta et al., 2009; Krieg et al., 1995; Nikitin et al., 2014) (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Elgueta et al., 2009, Krieg et al., 1995, and Nikitin et al., 2014, as well as data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: While EBV induced marked ABT-737 resistance (IC50 ~3–4 µM), both CpG and CD40L/IL-4 stimulated B cells were significantly more sensitive to ABT-737 (IC50 ~200 nM).
source: We found that, while EBV induced marked ABT-737 resistance (IC50 ~3–4 µM), both CpG and CD40L/IL-4 stimulated B cells were significantly more sensitive to ABT-737 (IC50 ~200 nM) (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Mitogen-stimulated proliferating B cells had increased caspase 3/7 activity and Annexin V positivity following ABT-737 treatment.
source: Consistently, mitogen-stimulated proliferating B cells had increased caspase 3/7 activity and Annexin V positivity following ABT-737 treatment (Figure 4F–G) while EBV-infected cells displayed only marginally increased activity above basal levels (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Resistance to BCL-2 antagonism is specific to EBV-induced proliferation.
source: These data strongly support the hypothesis that resistance to BCL-2 antagonism is specific to EBV-induced proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of EBV-infected and mitogen-stimulated cells.

claim: P3HR1 infection did not alter the sensitivity of CpG-treated proliferating B cells to ABT-737.
source: P3HR1 infection did not alter the sensitivity of CpG-treated proliferating B cells to ABT-737 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The prototypical transforming strain, B95-8, induced marked ABT-737 resistance in the presence or absence of CpG.
source: In contrast, the prototypical transforming strain, B95-8, induced marked ABT-737 resistance in the presence or absence of CpG (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: EBNA2 is a key determinant of the ABT-737 resistance phenotype.
source: These data implicate EBNA2 as a key determinant of the ABT-737 resistance phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the P3HR1 (EBNA2-deleted) data.

claim: At 2 days post-infection, P3HR1-infected cells express high levels of Wp-driven transcripts, but significantly less Cp-driven transcripts including EBNA2, EBNA3A, and EBNA3C relative to B95-8 infected cells.
source: At 2 days post-infection, a time point at which ABT-737 resistance first emerges (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), P3HR1-infected cells express high levels of Wp-driven transcripts, but significantly less Cp-driven transcripts including EBNA2, EBNA3A, and EBNA3C relative to B95-8 infected cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: P3HR1-infected cells expressed similar levels of BHRF1 as B95-8 infected cells.
source: We found that P3HR1-infected cells expressed similar levels of BHRF1 as B95-8 infected cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: BHRF1 was not associated with ABT-737 resistance in early-infected B cells.
source: Therefore, BHRF1 was not associated with ABT-737 resistance in early-infected B cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that P3HR1 and B95-8 express similar BHRF1 levels but differ in ABT-737 resistance.

claim: △3C-infected proliferating B cells were resistant to ABT-737 (IC50 ~3 µM) similar to WT B95-8-infected cells (IC50 ~4 µM).
source: While △3C-infected proliferating B cells were resistant to ABT-737 (IC50 ~3 µM) similar to WT B95-8-infected cells (IC50 ~4 µM), the △3A-infected proliferating B cells remained highly sensitive to ABT-737 (~200 nM) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: △3A-infected proliferating B cells remained highly sensitive to ABT-737 (~200 nM).
source: While △3C-infected proliferating B cells were resistant to ABT-737 (IC50 ~3 µM) similar to WT B95-8-infected cells (IC50 ~4 µM), the △3A-infected proliferating B cells remained highly sensitive to ABT-737 (~200 nM) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: △3A LCL exhibited enhanced sensitivity to ABT-737 (IC50 ~60 nM) and ABT-199 (IC50 ~180 nM) relative to a donor-matched WT LCL (IC50 ~4 µM).
source: Furthermore, from our initial infections we were able to derive a △3A LCL, similar to that reported by others (Hertle et al., 2009; Skalska et al., 2010), and we again observed enhanced sensitivity to ABT-737 and ABT-199 in the △3A LCL (IC50 ~60 nM and ~180 nM, respectively) relative to a donor-matched WT LCL (IC50 ~4 µM) (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, as well as citations to Hertle et al., 2009 and Skalska et al., 2010.

claim: The △3A LCL was sensitive to both the Bad and Bmf peptides indicating BCL-2 dependence and an absence of BFL-1 and MCL-1 protection similar to the uninfected B cell state.
source: We found that the △3A LCL, in contrast to WT, was sensitive to both the Bad and Bmf peptides indicating BCL-2 dependence and an absence of BFL-1 and MCL-1 protection similar to the uninfected B cell state (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by BH3 profiling data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: △3A LCLs expressed significantly less BFL-1 at the mRNA level, while the BCL-2 and MCL-1 mRNA levels were similar to WT, if not slightly elevated.
source: Mechanistically, we found that △3A LCLs expressed significantly less BFL-1 at the mRNA level, while the BCL-2 and MCL-1 mRNA levels were similar to WT, if not slightly elevated (Figure 6B and additional clones in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Loss of BFL-1 mRNA expression was not due to selective pressure applied during outgrowth of △3A LCL.
source: Loss of BFL-1 mRNA expression was not due to selective pressure applied during outgrowth of △3A LCL as EBNA3A-ERT2 fusion protein expressing LCLs lost or gained BFL-1 expression upon HT withdrawal or addition, respectively, in a stable LCL (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: MCL-1 mRNA, protein, and protein stability were unchanged in the △3A LCL compared to WT.
source: While BH3-profiling predicted a loss of MCL-1 activity, MCL-1 mRNA, protein, and protein stability were unchanged in the △3A LCL compared to WT (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: MCL-1 localization to mitochondria was defective in the △3A LCL.
source: Instead, we discovered that MCL-1 localization to mitochondria was defective in the △3A LCL (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: △3A LCLs were only transcribing ~15% as much BFL-1 mRNA as WT LCLs.
source: Indeed, when we isolated nascent mRNAs using a thiolated-RNA pull down method we found that △3A LCLs were only transcribing ~15% as much BFL-1 mRNA as WT LCLs (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by nascent transcription profiling data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Decreased BFL-1 transcription in △3A LCLs was correlated with decreased RNA polymerase II (Pol II), activated Pol II (phospho Serine 5), and activating histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K9ac, and H3K4me3) accumulating at the BFL-1 transcription start site (TSS).
source: Furthermore, we found that decreased BFL-1 transcription in △3A LCLs was correlated with decreased RNA polymerase II (Pol II), activated Pol II (phospho Serine 5), and activating histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K9ac, and H3K4me3) accumulating at the BFL-1 transcription start site (TSS) (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Two genomic regions upstream of the BFL-1 gene were strongly associated with the TSS in WT LCLs but less so in △3A LCLs.
source: We discovered two genomic regions upstream of the BFL-1 gene that were strongly associated with the TSS in WT LCLs but less so in △3A LCLs (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin conformation capture data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: One locus is bound by EBNA3A within a known EBV Super Enhancer (39 kb upstream of the BFL-1 TSS) and the other region contains a single RelA peak.
source: Using LCL ChIP-Seq data (Schmidt et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2011), we found that one locus is bound by EBNA3A within a known EBV Super Enhancer (39 kb upstream of the BFL-1 TSS) and the other region contains a single RelA peak, an NFκB transcription factor subunit strongly activated by LMP1 (Zhao et al., 2014) (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 6I and citations to Schmidt et al., 2015, Zhao et al., 2011, and Zhao et al., 2014.

claim: EBNA3A plays an important role in coordinating NFκB-mediated regulation of BFL-1 transcription in LCLs.
source: These data support an important new role for EBNA3A in coordinating NFκB-mediated regulation of BFL-1 transcription in LCLs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the chromatin conformation and ChIP-Seq data.

claim: EBNA3A re-expression was sufficient to restore ABT-737 resistance similar to WT LCLs.
source: We found that EBNA3A re-expression was sufficient to restore ABT-737 resistance similar to WT LCLs (Figure 6J–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6J-K.

claim: EBNA3A plays an important role in EBV-mediated resistance to BCL-2 antagonists and survival in response to potent proliferative signals during both early and late stages of B cell growth transformation.
source: Therefore, we conclude that EBNA3A plays an important role in EBV-mediated resistance to BCL-2 antagonists and survival in response to potent proliferative signals during both early and late stages of B cell growth transformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective data on EBNA3A function.

claim: EBV encodes two putative BCL-2 homologues that are not required for survival after the first 24 hr following B cell infection.
source: While EBV encodes two putative BCL-2 homologues, these proteins are not required for survival after the first 24 hr following B cell infection (Altmann and Hammerschmidt, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Altmann and Hammerschmidt, 2005.

claim: Constitutive NFκB signaling from the viral oncoprotein LMP1 is thought to be responsible for apoptotic suppression in latently infected, proliferating cells.
source: Rather, constitutive NFκB signaling from the viral oncoprotein LMP1, a TNFR homologue, is thought to be responsible for apoptotic suppression in latently infected, proliferating cells (Cahir-McFarland et al., 2000; Pratt et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cahir-McFarland et al., 2000 and Pratt et al., 2012.

claim: The initial burst of B cell proliferation induced by EBV is driven by expression of the viral EBNA transcription factors in the absence of appreciable LMP1 or NFκB activity.
source: However, the initial burst of B cell proliferation induced by EBV is driven by expression of the viral EBNA transcription factors (EBNA1, 2, 3A, 3B, 3C, and LP) in the absence of appreciable LMP1 or NFκB activity (Price et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Price et al., 2012.

claim: The early period of hyper-proliferation activates a growth-suppressive DNA damage response.
source: Furthermore, this early period of hyper-proliferation activates a growth-suppressive DNA damage response, which would be expected to promote apoptosis (Nikitin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nikitin et al., 2010.

claim: Mature human peripheral blood B cells depend solely on BCL-2 for survival.
source: In our BH3 profiling study, we found that mature human peripheral blood B cells depend solely on BCL-2 for survival while EBV latent infection further suppressed apoptotic priming during outgrowth by initially upregulating MCL-1, followed by BFL-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BH3 profiling data.

claim: EBV latent infection further suppressed apoptotic priming during outgrowth by initially upregulating MCL-1, followed by BFL-1.
source: In our BH3 profiling study, we found that mature human peripheral blood B cells depend solely on BCL-2 for survival while EBV latent infection further suppressed apoptotic priming during outgrowth by initially upregulating MCL-1, followed by BFL-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BH3 profiling data.

claim: EBNA3A regulates the BH3 profile of EBV-infected cells and suppresses apoptosis by promoting MCL-1 mitochondrial localization and increasing BFL-1 mRNA transcription.
source: EBNA3A regulated the BH3 profile of EBV-infected cells and suppressed apoptosis by promoting MCL-1 mitochondrial localization and increasing BFL-1 mRNA transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective data on EBNA3A function.

claim: Transcription of BFL-1 was previously shown to be regulated by the EBV transcription factor EBNA2 as well as LMP1-induced NFκB.
source: Transcription of BFL-1 was previously shown to be regulated by the EBV transcription factor EBNA2 (Pegman et al., 2006) as well as LMP1-induced NFκB (Pratt et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pegman et al., 2006 and Pratt et al., 2012.

claim: EBNA3A coordinates a chromatin architecture through an EBV super enhancer that facilitates NFκB-mediated activation of BFL-1 transcription.
source: Our work now indicates that EBNA3A coordinates a chromatin architecture through an EBV super enhancer that facilitates NFκB-mediated activation of BFL-1 transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chromatin conformation and ChIP data.

claim: The importance of MCL-1 in early EBV-infected human B cells is consistent with the critical role of MCL-1 in germinal center (GC) formation and memory B cell survival in the mouse.
source: The importance of MCL-1 in early EBV-infected human B cells coupled with the critical role of MCL-1 in germinal center (GC) formation and memory B cell survival in the mouse (Vikstrom et al., 2010) is consistent with the GC model of EBV infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vikstrom et al., 2010 and represents an inference connecting EBV biology to the GC model.

claim: The GC model posits that EBV infection of naïve B cells promotes B cell maturation mimicking the GC reaction to access the long-lived memory B cell compartment.
source: The GC model posits that EBV infection of naïve B cells promotes B cell maturation mimicking the GC reaction to access the long-lived memory B cell compartment and thus persisting for the lifetime of the host (Burns et al., 2015; Roughan and Thorley-Lawson, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burns et al., 2015 and Roughan and Thorley-Lawson, 2009.

claim: MCL-1 copy number gains and mutations are often found in B cell lymphomas.
source: Furthermore, MCL-1 copy number gains and mutations are often found in B cell lymphomas (Wenzel et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wenzel et al., 2013.

claim: The early phase of EBV infection where EBNAs are expressed with little or no expression of LMPs is known as latency IIb.
source: The early phase of EBV infection where EBNAs are expressed with little or no expression of LMPs is known as latency IIb (Price and Luftig, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Price and Luftig, 2015.

claim: The latency IIb expression pattern has been observed in EBV-positive HIV-associated lymphomas, post-transplant lymphomas, in acute infectious mononucleosis, and in tumors of humanized mouse models of EBV infection.
source: The latency IIb expression pattern has also been observed by immuno-histochemical analysis in EBV-positive HIV-associated lymphomas, post-transplant lymphomas, in acute infectious mononucleosis, and in tumors of humanized mouse models of EBV infection (Price and Luftig, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Price and Luftig, 2015.

claim: An EBV recombinant lacking LMP1 was capable of forming B cell tumors in a humanized mouse model.
source: Indeed, a recent study found that an EBV recombinant lacking LMP1 was capable of forming B cell tumors in a humanized mouse model (Ma et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ma et al., 2015.

claim: The survival of latency IIb expressing cells likely depends on EBNA3A and MCL-1, while latency III cells expressing LMP proteins and high level NFκB signaling are likely to be less primed and to rely on BFL-1.
source: The survival of these cells as well as those in other latency IIb expressing tissues likely depends on EBNA3A and MCL-1, while latency III cells expressing LMP proteins and high level NFκB signaling are likely to be less primed and to rely on BFL-1.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: BH3 profiling has been a powerful predictive tool for chemotherapeutic responses in leukemias.
source: As BH3 profiling has been a powerful predictive tool for chemotherapeutic responses in leukemias (Montero et al., 2015), our new findings suggest that such an approach could allow for better treatment decisions for EBV-associated malignancies.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Montero et al., 2015.

claim: BH3 profiling could allow for better treatment decisions for EBV-associated malignancies.
source: As BH3 profiling has been a powerful predictive tool for chemotherapeutic responses in leukemias (Montero et al., 2015), our new findings suggest that such an approach could allow for better treatment decisions for EBV-associated malignancies.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings of the study.
